Orgasmic Meditation and the Brain

What Dr. Andrew Newberg's brain-imaging research shows about how OM affects the brain, and what that means for its benefits · November 2026

Dr. Andrew Newberg, a neuroscientist at Thomas Jefferson University and a pioneer in the brain science of meditation and prayer, has published three peer-reviewed brain-imaging studies of orgasmic meditation (OM). Together they show OM producing a distinctive brain state: regions that maintain the sense of self, effortful control and self-judgment quiet down, while the body becomes energized and the brain systems that attune to another person become more engaged. The reward circuitry that drives sexual arousal stays largely out of it.

The OM brain state at a glance

The three studies

StudyWhat it measuredWho
Newberg et al. 2021, Frontiers in PsychologyfMRI brain connectivity shortly after the practice, plus heart rate and heart-rate variability20 experienced practitioner pairs, each doing OM and a neutral control session (leg stroking) on separate days in random order
Newberg et al. 2022/2023, F1000ResearchFDG-PET brain activity during the practice (a glucose tracer injected midway records where the brain uses energy)The same 20 pairs, same OM vs control design
Newberg et al. 2024, Frontiers in NeuroimagingResting FDG-PET brain activity40 long-term practitioners (over a year of regular practice) vs 19 non-meditators

These maps show the regions Newberg reported as changing during the practice, compared with the neutral leg-stroking session. Women receive the stimulation; men give it, and their brains respond differently.

Seven ways OM affects the brain

Newberg's findings group into seven brain systems. Each card shows the regions involved, what he found, and what it means based on his interpretation and the brain-function research he cites.

Less active during OMMore active / more connectedExpected to activate, did not
1

The sense of self and boundaries softens

What Newberg found

  • During the practice, activity drops in the superior and inferior parietal lobe, angular gyrus and precuneus, most strongly in women.
  • In women, the more intense the session, the lower the right superior parietal activity (r = −0.58).
  • Long-term practitioners show lower resting activity in the angular gyrus, inferior parietal lobe and precuneus.

What it means

These regions build the sense of where the body ends and the world begins. In Newberg's earlier studies of Buddhist meditators and praying nuns, reduced activity here accompanied feelings of oneness and a dissolving boundary between self and other. In OM, this is the brain-level match for what practitioners describe: merging with the partner and the experience. It also aligns with survey data in which 62% of practitioners reported a "complete" mystical experience during a powerful OM.

2

The "thinking and controlling" brain steps back

What Newberg found

  • During the practice, the middle and superior frontal cortex quiets in men; the left inferior frontal cortex quiets in women.
  • Long-term practitioners show lower resting frontal activity.

What it means

The frontal lobes run deliberate effort, planning and self-monitoring. Newberg's research shows frontal activity rises in effortful concentration and falls in practices of surrender or flow. The men, who give the stimulation, describe becoming absorbed or "lost" in the practice, which fits a frontal step-back. Researchers call this pattern transient hypofrontality, the same frontal release seen in flow states.

3

Self-monitoring and judgment quiet down

What Newberg found

  • Activity drops in the anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex during the practice.
  • Both are lower at rest in long-term practitioners.

What it means

The anterior cingulate is the brain's "am I doing this right?" monitor, tracking errors and conflict. The orbitofrontal cortex evaluates and inhibits. Lower activity in both points to less self-judgment and inhibition. Newberg notes the orbitofrontal decrease also appears at orgasm; in OM it occurs without climax, suggesting a release of self-evaluation without the sexual endpoint.

4

Body awareness is reshaped

What Newberg found

  • Insula activity drops overall during the practice.
  • In women, a more intense session goes with higher left insula activity (r = +0.60).
  • Long-term female practitioners show lower resting activity in the insula and thalamus.

What it means

The insula turns body sensation into felt emotion; the thalamus relays sensation to the rest of the brain. Intensity appears to depend on how much bodily sensation stays online while self-related processing quiets. Lower resting activity in long-term practitioners may reflect more efficient baseline processing of sensation and emotion, which Newberg links to emotional regulation.

5

Partners tune in to each other

What Newberg found

  • After the practice, the superior temporal lobe becomes more strongly connected with the insula, inferior frontal cortex and anterior cingulate.
  • In men, the supramarginal gyrus links more strongly with the cerebellum.
  • During the practice, brain changes in one partner correlated with brain changes in the other, and each partner's rated intensity tracked activity in the other partner's brain.

What it means

This network handles reading other people, empathy and social bonding; Newberg compares it to loving-kindness meditation, which builds compassion. The supramarginal gyrus processes touch and how one's movement affects another person, fitting the giver's role of staying closely attuned. The partner-to-partner correlations are the most distinctive result in this research: OM appears to produce a shared state between two people. That matches the closeness study, in which 125 pairs reported feeling closer after a single session.

6

The body is energized, not sedated

What Newberg found

  • Heart rate rises about 7.6 bpm in both partners (11 to 12%).
  • Heart-rate variability shifts toward sympathetic, "activated" tone.
  • The cerebellum is more active in men during the practice.

What it means

OM is an alert, energized state, closer to focused concentrative meditation than to relaxation practices. The cerebellum increase likely reflects the precise, coordinated hand movements the practice requires.

7

It works differently from sex

What Newberg found

Newberg expected increases in reward, emotion and sexual-response regions (basal ganglia, limbic areas, thalamus) during OM. They did not appear. The dominant pattern was deactivation.

What it means

Sexual arousal and orgasm light up the brain's reward circuitry broadly. OM produces a mostly quieting pattern while the body stays aroused. Newberg concludes OM is a "unique hybrid" of meditation and sexual stimulation, closer to meditation in how it affects the brain.

What changes with long-term practice

At rest, without practicing, long-term practitioners show lower activity across frontal, temporal and parietal regions, the anterior cingulate, insula and thalamus. These regions belong to networks that handle attention, salience (deciding what matters) and the brain's default, self-referential mode. Newberg interprets this as a "consolidation" of brain responses through repeated practice, a streamlining of the systems OM engages. Women showed lower resting activity especially in the thalamus and insula; men especially in the cerebellum and cingulate. Because the networks involved govern cognition, attention and emotional regulation, Newberg suggests these changes have implications for how OM affects practitioners over time.

What it adds up to

By Newberg's results, OM creates a state with three simultaneous parts:

  1. Quieting of the systems that maintain self-boundaries, effortful control and self-judgment: the meditative element.
  2. Activation of the body and of the systems that attune to another person: the partnered element.
  3. No pull from the reward circuitry that drives sexual arousal and orgasm.

Over time, the same networks appear to settle into a lower resting baseline. Because they govern attention, emotional regulation and the sense of self, Newberg suggests OM could have therapeutic uses for conditions involving those systems, such as anxiety, depression and trauma.

From brain findings to benefits

Newberg's studies measure the brain. A separate set of OM studies measures outcomes. The table connects each benefit to its evidence and to the brain findings above.

BenefitEvidenceStrengthBrain link
Sense of oneness, transcendence or mystical experienceSiegel & Emmert-Aronson 2021: 780 practitioners scored a powerful past OM on a validated mystical-experience scale; 62% met the threshold for a "complete" mystical experience. In 56 pairs rating their next OM, 23% did, and partners' scores tracked each other.Moderate
Large samples, validated scale; self-selected practitioners, no comparison group.		Strongest link. The women's parietal/precuneus drop is the region most tied to self-boundary loss in meditation and prayer research. Men, who give the stimulation, showed no parietal change.
Feeling closer to a partnerPrause, Siegle & Coan 2021 (PLOS ONE): 125 pairs rated closeness before and after one OM. Closeness rose on average, more in non-romantic pairs than romantic ones.Moderate
Decent sample; measured right after a single session, no control activity.		Plausible: increased temporal–insula–cingulate coupling after OM involves social and empathy regions. Not tested together in the same people.

Immediate effect only; no lasting mood measure.		Partial: the absence of reward-circuit activation suggests the pleasure works differently from orgasm. Mechanism unclear.

PTSD scores fell from 60.9 to 26.7 (PCL-5), anxiety from 19.2 to 10.0 (GAD-7), depression from 20.2 to 10.9 (PHQ-9). No one withdrew for safety reasons.Preliminary
No control group, small sample, unverified home practice, run at the funder's request. The authors note placebo and attention effects cannot be ruled out.		Speculative: insula and default-mode regions are implicated in PTSD, and both shift during OM. No imaging was done in a clinical group.

Cross-sectional, possible pre-existing differences, reporting anomalies.		N/A: it is unclear whether lower resting activity is beneficial.
Relaxation or stress reduction during the practiceHeart-rate and HRV data (Newberg 2021); skin conductance (Siegle & Prause 2022).ContradictedThe body becomes more activated during OM, not less. Any calming benefit would come afterward, which no study has measured physiologically.

The most defensible summary: OM reliably produces a pleasant, activated state that practitioners describe as connected and self-transcendent, and the brain shows a matching quieting of the regions that maintain the sense of self. Closeness and mood benefits are measured but short-term. Mental-health benefits are promising and would be confirmed by a trial comparing OM with another activity.

Appendix: notes on the data

The raw PET scans from Newberg's F1000 study are publicly available (Figshare, CC0). An independent reanalysis of those scans was run for this report.

  • Agreement: the reanalysis reproduces the overall direction of Newberg's results (mostly decreases during OM, cerebellum increases); its brain map correlates 0.48 with his published map.
  • Strongest finding: the women's parietal and precuneus decrease (system 1) survives the strictest available statistical correction, in 16 of 17 women. This is the most robust result in the dataset.
  • Other regions: under that stricter correction, the remaining regions do not reach significance at this sample size. They appear at Newberg's threshold and in the same direction, so they are best read as consistent but awaiting larger studies.
  • Dataset notes: the public files contain 38 subjects rather than the 40 reported; one file labeled as a brain scan is a torso scan and one scan is cut off at the top of the head. Both were excluded from the reanalysis.

All three studies were funded by the Institute of OM Foundation and declare no conflicts of interest. The function of a region is inferred from the broader brain-imaging literature, as is standard in this field.
